extracted.intended_audience: research funders, policy-makers, and researchers studying grant peer review and research funding systems
extracted.subtask_description: Synthesis and evaluation of dimensions used to judge the effectiveness, fairness, burden, and design of grant peer review systems; aimed at informing funders and researchers about evidence, biases, and possible improvements. Covers empirical findings and proposed interventions (blinding, lotteries, shortened applications, portfolio approaches, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Gender bias in peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether peer review outcomes differ by applicant gender (e.g. studies finding men more likely to be approved). Evidence is conflicting: some studies/meta-analyses suggest men are more likely to be funded (Bornmann et al. 2007 found men 7% more likely), while other reviews (Ceci & Williams 2011) find peer review fair across gender.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret findings cautiously: aggregation over fields/cohorts may produce effects; cohort changes over time may influence results. Use careful modelling that accounts for cohort and field. Multiple large-scale and meta-analytic studies give mixed conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Age bias / bias against early career researchers
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether applicant age or career stage affects grant success. Concerns that processes relying on prior publications or funding will disadvantage early career researchers; evidence is mixed (some studies find no direct age impact, others find declining success with age).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider policy levers (e.g. NIH measures equalizing success rates for new vs established investigators) and examine whether eligibility or review criteria implicitly disadvantage early career applicants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cronyism and conflicts of interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether prior affiliation or social connections between applicants and reviewers/panelists increases funding chances. Evidence includes Wenneras & Wold (1997) and other studies finding affiliation increases success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Funders should have detailed conflict-of-interest processes; evaluate whether panel composition, panelists' own application patterns, or deference to experts enable cronyism. Distinguish between genuine expertise effects and nepotism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cognitive particularism / disciplinary bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Tendency for reviewers to favour proposals from their own field or school of thought (i.e. favouring familiar topics or ways of thinking), which can bias direction of funded research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Possible mitigations include broadening the range of scientific problems judged by each group, including diverse fields on panels, and using senior scientists with wide appreciation to counter specialist overvaluation. But balance this against the value of expertise — evaluators closer to an area may better assess quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Field-specific bias (discipline advantage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Systematic differences in funding success across fields (e.g. proposals in molecular biology having higher success rates than other bioscience fields).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyse cross-field differences and consider panel composition, scoring norms, and the possibility that some fields are 'favoured' by review cultures or metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness of peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: How long peer review takes (noted as 9–18 months from submission to funding) and whether these delays meaningfully hinder research progress, translation to practice, or responses to urgent events (e.g. epidemics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure time-to-decision and time-to-funding; weigh peer review delays against other steps in translation (research-to-practice often ~17 years). Consider rapid review pathways for time-sensitive work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stakeholder support and perceived legitimacy
rubrics_metrics.description: The extent to which major scientific stakeholders (researchers, institutions, funders) support and trust peer review procedures. Empirical evidence suggests strong support despite criticisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize disconnects between institutional/community confidence and empirical effectiveness; consider stakeholder perceptions when designing reforms and communicate transparently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall burden of peer review on the research system
rubrics_metrics.description: Aggregate costs (time, money, administrative effort) of preparing, reviewing, and administering grant applications; evidence indicates increasing burden over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantify total burden and trends (e.g. surveys across funders). Use burden estimates to evaluate reforms intended to reduce costs or redistribute effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution of burden (applicants vs reviewers vs funders)
rubrics_metrics.description: How the monetised/time burden is split: studies report majority falls on applicants (estimates 74–85% for application production), with reviewers/panel members and administration making up smaller shares.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize applicant burden reduction or increase applicant value from the process; measure burdens empirically rather than assume they follow a fixed distribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monetised cost estimates of application preparation
rubrics_metrics.description: Monetary estimates of cost per grant or percentage of budgets consumed by application processes (examples: NHMRC $14,000 per grant; RCUK 10–17% of research costs; estimates vary and are contested).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious interpreting disputed estimates (e.g. NSERC debate); transparency about assumptions (time taken, hourly rates, overhead allocation) is essential when presenting monetary estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application complexity and length
rubrics_metrics.description: The required length and complexity of applications (examples: 80–120 page applications, NIH R01 reduced from 25 to 12 pages) and their relation to burden and decision quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical tests show shortening applications can reduce administrative burden but may not reduce applicant preparation time (applicants may invest a fixed proportion of time). Pilot and evaluate changes carefully; watch for unintended effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliability and reproducibility of peer review decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Consistency of reviewer ratings and panel decisions (e.g. inter-assessor correlations, variability across stages). Evidence of inconsistency and poor predictive validity for future performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capture measures of inter-rater reliability and reproducibility; acknowledge uncertainty in decisions. Use reproducibility metrics when assessing review system performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bias against innovation
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence that peer review tends to disfavour innovative or high-risk research, limiting novel directions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider specific evaluation criteria or selection mechanisms to protect innovative proposals (e.g. portfolio approaches, adjusting scoring to value novelty) and test interventions empirically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cognitive distance effects
rubrics_metrics.description: How intellectual distance between reviewers' expertise and proposals affects judgments (reviewers may favour either very familiar or very unfamiliar areas; mixed findings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure cognitive distance in panels and use it as an explanatory variable for disagreement; consider mixing reviewers to cover a range of distances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blinding / anonymisation of applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of blinded reviews to reduce identity-based biases; feasibility is debated and results mixed (short anonymised vs full proposals showed weak correlations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trial blinding where possible, but assess feasibility (some proposal content reveals identity) and measure effects on outcomes and reviewer behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer training to reduce bias and improve review quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Training programmes for reviewers aimed at reducing bias (e.g. CIHR, NIH) and improving review consistency; limited evidence suggests some benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement and evaluate training interventions; monitor whether training reduces discrepancies or improves predictive validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capturing reviewer confidence and expressing uncertainty
rubrics_metrics.description: Asking reviewers to provide both a rating and a measure of confidence in that rating to acknowledge uncertainty and improve decision-making/analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use confidence scores to identify high-disagreement or high-uncertainty proposals; consider disagreement as a signal of potential innovation. Funders (e.g. Villum and Velux) have started implementing such systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portfolio-based selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Selecting a mix of projects that score highly across diverse criteria (including innovation) to reduce reliance on fine-grained ranking and to diversify funded research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate portfolio selection strategies against single-metric ranking; monitor diversity and outcomes over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introducing randomness / lottery mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Using random allocation (full lottery or lotteries within selected groups) to reduce biases and the need for fine-grained discrimination among similarly ranked proposals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider hybrid models (identify fundable pool then randomise). Random selection reduces some biases but eligibility rules can reintroduce bias; politically challenging though piloted in a few cases (Explorer Grants, Seed Projects, Experiment! Grants).

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-threshold randomisation approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposal to fund all applications above a higher threshold, reject all below a lower threshold, and randomise funding for applications between thresholds (blurring the funding line).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reduces the need for exact ranking near the cutoff; simulate and pilot to evaluate impacts on fairness and perceived legitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shortened application / triage processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of short preliminary applications with triage (e.g. NSF's 75% cull rate) to reduce workload and focus resources on promising proposals; studies found simplified processes could achieve ~75% agreement with standard decisions and save substantial review costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure agreement thresholds you consider acceptable (e.g. ~75% used in some studies) and estimate cost-savings vs potential loss of accuracy; evaluate across contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Optimal number of reviewers (trade-off with reproducibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Statistical estimation of the number of reviewers that balances improved reproducibility with reviewer burden (studies suggest optimal numbers around five in one analysis, 11 in another).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat optimal reviewer count as context-dependent; model trade-offs and pilot different reviewer counts while monitoring reproducibility and resource use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review by applicants (applicant-as-reviewer models)
rubrics_metrics.description: Models where applicants review each other's proposals (e.g. NSF pilot where each applicant completed seven reviews), reducing burden on funders and increasing the number of reviews per proposal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guard against strategic marking by rewarding alignment with other reviewers; assess whether increased review counts and removal of panels affect decision quality and fairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Providing feedback to applicants
rubrics_metrics.description: Offering reviewer and panel feedback to applicants to increase the value of applying (but with concerns that feedback may invite appeals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider benefits of feedback for applicant learning and community value; balance against legal/administrative risks and implement clear policies on feedback scope and appeals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of technology / remote review
rubrics_metrics.description: Using remote review and online processes to reduce time and travel burden; evidence suggests outcomes remain similar but face-to-face panels provide side-benefits (networking, social interactions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ technology to reduce cost while planning alternative ways to preserve networking and informal benefits if face-to-face is reduced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative proposal formats (multi-media/video)
rubrics_metrics.description: Changing application formats to include multimedia or video to improve information transmission and potentially reduce burden, though effects are untested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pilot novel formats and rigorously evaluate their effects on review quality, accessibility, and burden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for stronger evidence base and transparent evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: The paucity of robust studies on peer review effectiveness and design; funders should experiment, evaluate, publish results, and make data available for analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build before-and-after comparisons for reforms, publish methods and data, and collaborate across funders for comparative analyses; be willing to share sensitive data under appropriate safeguards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study of social processes in panel discussions
rubrics_metrics.description: The importance of researching how panel deliberations and social dynamics shape decisions — currently almost no studies examine these processes despite their centrality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design observational or cooperative studies with funders to analyse panel meetings; expect challenges around confidentiality and funder sensitivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of system-level interactions and modelling
rubrics_metrics.description: Understanding peer review requires considering systemic factors (funding levels, researcher demographics) and their interactions; modelling and simulation approaches can help.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use system dynamics, agent-based models, and simulations to study interactions between policy changes, funding supply, applicant behaviour, and review design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and data availability
rubrics_metrics.description: Funders should make data available for analysis and openly publish evaluations of their processes to enable improvement and comparative research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop policies and mechanisms to publish anonymised datasets and evaluation results, balancing transparency with confidentiality concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact of falling success rates on perceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Declining funding success rates amplify dissatisfaction with peer review and compound applicant burden.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for macro-level funding context when interpreting critiques of peer review; consider whether reforms should address funding levels and distribution, not only review mechanics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade-off between burden reduction and decision quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Changes intended to reduce burden (shorter applications, fewer reviewers) must be evaluated for their effect on decision reproducibility and quality; some experiments show simplified processes can achieve acceptable agreement while saving costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set explicit acceptability thresholds for agreement and decision fidelity; pilot reforms with before/after measurement and cost-benefit analysis.
